draft.title: Multiplying along branches
card: Each branch of a tree diagram has a probability. The probability of one path is found by multiplying the probabilities along its branches.
Example: a bag has 3 red and 2 blue counters. Draw one, put it back, then draw again. \(P(\text{red, then red}) = \frac{3}{5} \times \frac{3}{5} = \frac{9}{25}\).
Some events can happen by more than one path. Find the probability of each path that gives the event, then add them.

Example: for one red and one blue in any order, the paths are red then blue, and blue then red. \(\frac{3}{5} \times \frac{2}{5} + \frac{2}{5} \times \frac{3}{5} = \frac{6}{25} + \frac{6}{25} = \frac{12}{25}\).
draft.remember: Multiply along a path. Add the paths that make the event.

a.q: Mei spins a spinner twice. Each spin lands on green with probability \(\frac{1}{4}\). What is \(P(\text{green, then green})\)?
a.why: Along one path, multiply: \(\frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{16}\). Adding gives \(\frac{1}{2}\), which is the tempting mistake, but adding is only for combining different paths.
a.clue: One path, so which operation joins its branches?

b.q: A bag has 2 red and 3 blue counters. Jo draws one, replaces it, then draws again. What is the probability that the two counters are different colours?
b.why: Two paths give different colours: red then blue is \(\frac{2}{5} \times \frac{3}{5} = \frac{6}{25}\), and blue then red is also \(\frac{6}{25}\). Add them to get \(\frac{12}{25}\). Using only one path gives \(\frac{6}{25}\) and misses the other order.
b.clue: Different colours can happen in two orders.
